Plant the Moon Challenge | Spring 2024 | Professional/Undergraduate Division 
Minnesota West Bluejays C Team # 17985 
Minnesota West Community & Technical College | Worthington, MN 
Grant Funded by NASA’s Minnesota Space Grant Consortium 
 
Elijah Alexander, DaShawn Clark, Olivia Hensch, Diego Montoya, Terrence Pierre, 
Elijah Robinson, Adrian Sanchez, Fanuel Wolday, and Heidi Tarus

2 
Introduction 
The main driving question for the Plant the Moon Challenge (PTMC; 
https://plantthemoon.com/) is to contribute to the growing body of knowledge to determine 
how humans can grow high yield and nutrient rich crops on a Moon colony. A sister challenge 
called the Plant Mars challenge is also available; however, because Minnesota West teams have 
been working on the Plant the Moon Challenge for almost two years, this semester’s C team 
determined to continue with the lunar regolith. The team was also interested in PTMC because 
of NASA’s Artemis project which aims to launch Artemis III which will send humans to explore 
the South Pole of the moon by September 2026. In tandem with humans’ return to the moon; 
NASA is interested in learning as much as they can about how to start a colony on the Moon. 
This includes learning about and researching how to sustainably support people by meeting 
their basic needs including access to nutritious food. One way to sustainably grow food is to use 
the natural resources provided by the Moon while limiting the amount of resources needed to 
be transported to the Moon. The biggest natural resource on the Moon is lunar regolith. The 
team is interested in using lunar regolith and investigating possible nutrient additives that can 
be added to the soil mixture to produce the highest yield of nutrient rich crops to feed 
individuals living on the moon. 
Theory 
Nitrogen, phosphorus, and calcium are essential macronutrients for plants. Nitrogen is 
used in the synthesis of proteins, nucleic acids, and some vitamins needed for growth, 
phosphorus is used for the synthesis of nucleic acids and phospholipids, and calcium is used to 
regulate nutrient transport, build cell walls, and support enzyme function (Clark et al., 2018). 
Based on research into organic farming, one way to add nitrogen, phosphorus, and calcium to 
the soil is to add bone meal (2% nitrogen, 17% phosphorus, 12% calcium). Bone meal is made 
from grinding up animal bones where it decomposes naturally in the soil to release nitrogen, 
phosphorus, and calcium along with micronutrients including magnesium, zinc, and iron (Puisis, 
2022). The nutrients not only have to be available in the soil, but they need to be absorbed by 
the roots of the plant. Nutrient acquisition can be increased by adding mycorrhizal fungi to the 
soil. The mycorrhizal fungi form a symbiotic relationship where the plant provides sugar to the

3 
fungi and the fungi help the plant with nutrient uptake. The lunar regolith lacks organic 
nutrients and mycorrhizal fungi – therefore the addition of bone meal and/or mycorrhizal fungi 
may benefit plants. The team used Dynomyco mycorrhizal inoculate which contains 700 
propagules/g of Glomus intraradices (aka Rhizophagus irregularis) and 200 propagules/g of 
Glomus mosseae. 
Based on the chosen additives, the team decided to plant a highly nutritious calorie rich 
plant that establishes a symbiotic relationship with mycorrhizal fungi - the mung bean (Vigna 
radiata). Mung bean seeds/beans can be easily cooked or sprouted and are a high calorie, 
nutritious, low fat food with 1 tbsp (13g) containing 45 calories, 3.11g protein, 8.14g 
carbohydrate with 2.12g fiber and only 0.15g of fat (USDA, 2019). Mung beans are popular in 
Asia and are gaining popularity in the United States with Oklahoma growing the largest share in 
the United States (Puisis, 2022). Prior mung bean research has been done using the fungi 
included in the Dynomyco mycorrhizal inoculate (Habibzadeh et al., 2013) and one of the 
species (G. mosseae) has been shown to be a common mycorrhizal fungus that associates with 
mung bean roots (Javaid & Kahn, 2019). 
For this experiment, the independent variable is the added bone meal and/or 
mycorrhizal inoculated to the soil mixture. The dependent variables for this study included 
germination rate, soil pH, plant height, and number of leaves. In addition, the team planned to 
include final root biomass and photosynthetic rate. These measurements were chosen to 
measure the success of plant germination and to measure the growth of the mung bean plants 
(Vigna radiata). We hypothesized that mung beans (Vigna radiata) grown in the pots containing 
both bone meal and the mycorrhizal inoculant would produce the tallest plants, have the most 
leaves, and would have the largest root biomass. In addition, the mung beans (Vigna radiata) 
grown in the pots containing both bone meal and the mycorrhizal inoculant would have the 
highest photosynthetic rate.

4 
Experiment & Measurement Methods 
Initial Set-Up 
The team used the following experimental design for this experiment: 
 
One week before the start of the grow period on Wednesday, February 7th, the soil was mixed 
with a volume ratio of 50% lunar regolith, 25% top soil, and 25% peat moss. Top soil was added to 
provide some organic material to the plants and the peat moss was added to help with moisture 
retention. The Fall 2023 Minnesota West Bluejay teams struggled with plant mortality due to the 
omission of peat moss which caused the plants to dry out quickly, so the team decided to add peat moss 
into the soil mixture to reduce this mortality. After the soil was mixed and placed in the 20 pots, the 
pots were labeled using colored popsicle sticks placed in the back of the pot - blue for control, purple 
bone meal, green for fungi, and yellow for bone meal & fungi. Next, the appropriate addition of either 
bone meal and or fungi was added based on pot size and the suggested quantity from the packaging of 
10lbs per 100sq ft of bone meal from the Earth Science Natural Bone Meal package and the suggested 
application of 5 g of Dynomyco mycorrhizal inoculant per 0.5 liters (see experimental design diagram for

5 
specific amounts). The additives were added on top and mixed into the top half of the soil. After the 
mixing, all pots were watered with 100ml of tap water. 
During the first week of the growing period on Thursday, February 8th, the eight students on the 
C Team paired up and picked one pot from each of the treatment groups with the fifth pot set taken by 
the advisor. The advisor and the pairs of students wrote an identifier on their popsicle sticks – “HT”, “DF 
FW”, “E, A”, “EA + DC”, “Dream Team”. Each pot was planted with three mung bean seeds and watered 
with 100ml of tap water. Over the course of the grow period, the set-up was kept under a grow light 
containing two 18” GE plant and aquarium bulbs on a 12-hour light: 12-hour dark timer at a 
temperature of 22°C. The grow light was placed 20 cm from the top of the table which is 12cm from the 
top of the pot. The close placement of the light was done to reduce possible legginess in the seedlings 
from having the grow light placed to far away from the germinating seedlings. 
 
 
 
Plant Care 
Each pot was watered with 50ml of tap water on Monday and Thursday each week 
during the grow period. Due to the amazing fast growth rate of the plants, the grow light was 
moved up from 20cm to 25cm from the table on Monday, February 19th (no picture available) 
to 30cm on Monday, February 26th, and to the final height of 35cm on Monday March 4th.

The plants were kept in the same spot and in the same room through the duration of 
the experiment and were moved away for the light source for a maximum of two hours on 
Thursday each week between 1pm and 3pm to take measurements and then replaced back in 
the same location after measuring. The experiment was cut short by one week due to the 
advisor being out of town during the last week of the grow period. 
Measurements 
Weekly measurements included soil pH, primordial leaf emergence for germination rate, 
plant height, and number of true leaves. Additional planned measurements were root biomass 
and photosynthetic rate; however, this was not collected during the last week of the grow 
period due to the instructor/advisor being out of town. Primordial leaf emergence was used to 
collect data on germination rate of the plants. Germination rate data was collected twice by 
visually observing of the number of germinated seeds 7 days (week 2) and 14 days (week 3). 
The soil pH, plant height, and number of true leaves was collected by team members once a 
week on Thursday using the tallest plant in the pot. Tools used included the soil pH meter sent 
with the lunar regolith, a 15-cm ruler, and eventually a meter stick for seven weeks. A top-view 
and side-view picture of the entire set-up was taken once a week on Thursday (Appendix B: 
Photos). Data was kept on paper data tables located next to the plants with the data entered 
into Microsoft Excel each week for data analysis. 
Analysis & Results 
The results section was completed using a provided template by the advisor/instructor for 
instructional purposes and analysis consistency. Data was organized and stored in a Microsoft Excel file 
where the graphs were produced, and average and standard errors were calculated. All other statistics 
including the Shapiro-Wilks test for normality, Kruskal-Wallis H tests for data showing a departure from 
normality, and the one-way ANOVA test for normal data were done using Statistics Kingdom 
(https://www.statskingdom.com/). 
Soil pH 
The soil pH fluctuated between 7.5 and 8 over the course of the seven weeks in the four 
different treatment groups (Figure 2). The soil became slightly more basic (increased pH) in all of the 
pots from week 1 to week 2. Based on the final pot pH, A Shapiro-Wilk tests showed a significance 
departure from the normality for the control group, W(5) = .55, p = .003, the bone meal group, W(5) =

7 
.68, p = .019, the fungi group, W(5) = .55, p = .003, and the bone meal & fungi group, W(5) = infinity, p = 
<.001. Because the data did not show normality for all four groups, a Kruskal-Wallis H test was used to 
analyze the between group data. The Kruskal-Wallis H test indicated that there was a non-significant 
difference in the soil pH between the four treatment groups, χ2(3) = 2.37, p = .498, with a mean rank 
score of 10.5 for the control group, 10.5 for the bone meal group, 8.5 for the fungi group, 10.5 for the 
bone meal & fungi group. 
 
Germination Rate 
Germination rate was measured by the primordial leaf emergence and was not influenced by 
the additives either in week 2 or in week 3 (Figure 3 and Figure 4). The team was impressed by the 
germination rate for this experiment because each pot in each treatment had at least one plant on 
which to collect data. For the week 2 germination rate, the Shapiro-Wilk tests showed a significance 
departure from the normality for the control group, W(5) = .68, p = .019, the fungi group, W(5) = .68, p = 
.019, and the bone meal & fungi group, W(5) = .68, p = .019; however, there was not a significant 
departure from normality for the bone meal group, W(5) = .88, p = .386. Because the data did not show 
normality for all four groups, a Kruskal-Wallis H test was used to analyze the between group data. The 
Kruskal-Wallis H test indicated that there was a non-significant difference in the germination rate 
between the four groups, χ2(3) = 0.68, p = .878, with a mean rank score of 12.1 for the control group, 
9.4 for the bone meal group, 10.4 for the fungi group, 10.1 for the bone meal & fungi group.

For the week 3 germination rate, the Shapiro-Wilk tests showed a significance departure from 
the normality for the control group, W(5) = .68, p = .019, the bone meal group, W(5) = .68, p = .019, the 
fungi group, W(5) = .55, p = .003, and the bone meal & fungi group, W(5) = .68, p = .019. Because the 
data did not show normality for all four groups, a Kruskal-Wallis H test was used to analyze the between 
group data. The Kruskal-Wallis H test indicated that there was a non-significant difference in the 
germination rate between the four groups, χ2(3) = 0.63, p = .890, with a mean rank score of 10 for the 
control group, 10 for the bone meal group, 12 for the fungi group, 10 for the bone meal & fungi group.

9 
Plant Height Growth Rate 
The team was awestruck by the plant growth in this experiment and were excited each week to 
check the plant height and to move up the grow light because the plants were exceeding expectations. 
Based on the experiment, plant height was influence by the addition of the additive to the pot (Figure 
5). For the final plant height growth, the Shapiro-Wilk test showed there was not a significant departure 
from normality for the control group, W(5) = .83, p = .180, the bone meal group, W(5) = .96, p = .964, 
the fungi group, W(5) = .91, p = .568, or the bone meal & fungi group, W(5) = .88, p = .360. Because the 
groups showed normality, a one-way ANOVA was performed to evaluate the relationship between the 
treatment groups and final plant height. The ANOVA was significant at the 0.05 level, F(3, 16) =4.6667, p 
= 0.01583. Tukey’s HSD Test for multiple comparisons found that the mean value of final plant height 
was significantly different between the control group and the bone meal group and the fungi group and 
the bone meal group. There was no statistically significant difference in the final plant height between 
any of the other groups.

Number of True Leaves 
Based on the experiment, the final number of true leaves was influence by the addition of the 
additive to the pot (Figure 6). For the final number of true leaves, the Shapiro-Wilk test showed a 
significant departure from normality for the control group, W(5) = Infinity , p = <0.001, the bone meal 
group, W(5) = Infinity , p = <0.001, the fungi group, = .55, p = ..003, and the bone meal & fungi group, 
W(5) = .55, p = .003. Because the data did not show normality for all four groups, a Kruskal-Wallis H test 
was used to analyze the between group data. The Kruskal-Wallis H test indicated that there is significant 
difference in the germination rate between the four groups, χ2(3) = 12.92, p = .005, with a mean rank 
score of 5.5 for the control group, 15.5 for bone meal group, 7.5 for the fungi group, and 13.5 for the 
bone meal & fungi group. The Post-Hoc Dunn's test using a Bonferroni corrected alpha of 0.0083 
indicated that the mean rank of the following pair is significantly different: the control group compared 
to the bone meal group.

Other Observations 
During measurements on the fourth week of the grow period, the team noticed that the leaves 
in the control group and the fungi group were a lighter color green compared to a darker color green in 
the bone meal group and the bone meal & fungi group. Although this was not measured in any way, the 
color difference is thought to be significant in terms of the health, growth, and function of the plants.

Discussion & Conclusion 
The team did not have hypothesis for the soil pH or the germination rate; however, the team 
understand the significance of collecting and reporting the data. The soil pH fluctuated between an 
average pH of 7.44 and 8 for the treatments over the seven weeks. It is noteworthy that the overall soil 
pH was lower the first week compared to the following weeks. The team is unsure if this is because of 
the learning curve of using and reading the pH scale on the provided pH meter or if this change from 
week 1 to week 2 is significant. Further investigation into replicating these results is needed to better 
understand the importance in the change. The average soil pH during the experiment is higher than the 
suggest pH for the growth of mung beans which is more acidic at a pH of 6.3 to 7.2 (Brillon, 2023). 
Including common gardening additives such as elemental sulfur, aluminum sulfate, or sulfuric acid to 
lower the soil pH would be a crucial experiment to see if the pH of the soil influences the growth of the 
mung bean plants. Another possible limitation in this experiment is the availability of the phosphorus 
from the bone meal to the mung bean plants as the team learned that phosphorus is only available to 
plants in acidic soil (Puisis, 2022). 
The team was excited about the successful germination rate experiment with all the pot having 
at least one seed germinate with many of the pots having all three seeds germinate. The germination 
rate was not different between the treatment groups showing that the additives did not influence the 
seed germination success. A reliable and high germination rate for crops is important to demonstrate in 
these experiments because people would be relying on the consistency of crop growth for survival in a 
Moon colony, especially with mung bean at it can take up to 100 days for the plant to become mature to 
produce the bean pods. The failure of a crop to grow and mature for people living on the Moon would 
be a matter of life and death depending on the amount and reliability of other crops available for 
consumption. 
The team hypothesized that mung beans (Vigna radiata) grown in the pots containing both 
bone meal and the mycorrhizal inoculant would produce the tallest plants, have the most leaves, and 
would have the largest root biomass. In addition, the mung beans (Vigna radiata) grown in the pots 
containing both bone meal and the mycorrhizal inoculant would have the highest photosynthetic rate. 
The photosynthetic rate was not measured as the advisor/instructor was out of town during the last 
week of the experiment when the data was schedule to be collected. The data collected during this 
experiment did not support the hypotheses. The plants in the bone meal treatment grew significantly 
taller and produced significantly more leaves compared to the control group and the fungi group. The 
bone meal & fungi group was not significantly different from the other three groups for either

13 
measurement although the plants showed a trend of being taller and producing more leaves over the 
control and fungi group. 
These results match part of Cheng’s (2017) finding that the addition of mycorrhizal fungi caused 
lower growth in mung bean plants when no fertilizer was added to the soil. This is due to the 
competition of the mycorrhizal fungi for nutrients with the plants causing plant growth to be reduced 
due to nutrient deficiencies. However, the results of this study, do not match the other finding by Cheng 
(2017) where the mycorrhizal fungi increased the plant growth in higher fertilizer environments. The 
lack of an increase in growth in the bone meal & fungi group could be due to the low amount of 
nutrients included in the bone meal that contains 2% nitrogen, 17% phosphorus, 12% calcium, and 0% 
potassium. Although the bone meal is close in nitrogen and phosphorus percent to the suggested 
fertilizer for mung beans of 5% nitrogen, 10% phosphorus, and 10% potassium (Brillon, 2023). Potassium 
was not added in this experiment which would be another macronutrient worth investigating as 
potassium is important for opening and closing of the stomata in the leaves to allow gas exchanged 
needed for photosynthesis (Clark et al., 2018). Additionally, there is the possibility that the added fungi 
species - Glomus intraradices (Rhizophagus irregularis) and Glomus mosseae did not form a symbiotic 
relationship with the mung bean roots. To investigate this further, the team suggests to collect root 
biomass and to make microscopic observations with a simple ink and vinegar soak assay on the roots as 
used in Cheng (2017) to observe if the mycorrhizal fungi formed a symbiotic relationship with the mung 
bean plants. 
 
An interesting observation during the experiment was the difference in the leaf colors where 
the control and fungi group had light green/yellow leaves compared to the dark green leaves on the 
plants in the bone meal and bone meal & fungi group. After some investigation, the team decided that 
the plants in the control and fungi only group showed a nitrogen deficiency. In a nitrogen deficiency the 
older leaves are affect first and show a yellowing with the new leaves showing a pale green color due to 
the lack of nitrogen that is important in the synthesis of the green protein chlorophyll essential to 
photosynthesis (Earth Juice, n.d. and Dubaniewicz, 2021). Evidence for a nitrogen deficiency was 
surprising because of the low amount of nitrogen available in the bone meal (2%) and because mung 
beans are a legume that are able to fix their own nitrogen with the help of nitrogen fixing bacteria. It is 
possible that the nitrogen fixing bacteria were not available in the top soil added to the lunar regolith 
and thus the symbiotic relationship did not develop in the control and fungi groups. Nitrogen fixation is 
costly to plants as it uses a significant amount of energy and stress (low water, low temperature, low 
nutrients) can reduce nitrogen fixation; therefore, Flyn & Idowu (2015) recommend the addition of

14 
nitrogen for legumes especially in sandy or low organic matter soils (such as the soil used in this 
experiment) to allow the plants time to establish the symbiotic relationship and start the fixation 
process. The team suggest future researchers to measure the leaf color as a proxy for chlorophyll 
production by using a qualitative leaf color chart similar to what is used for rice and corn or a more 
quantitative measurement such as the one developed by Kasajima (2019) called ‘Spectrometric Color 
Measurement’ (SCM) which measures the visible light in 5nm intervals and multiplied by either RGB or 
SYZ color values to obtain respective intensities or another alternative using photographs called 
‘Photographic Color Measurment’ (PCM) to get RBG values. The team also found an application called 
Petiole Pro that can measure chlorophyll content in leaves using a smartphone (Kuzmenko, 2021). 
 
Overall, the team recommends the use of bone meal as a possible additive to lunar regolith for 
the growth of mung beans. One disadvantage is the weight and amount of bone meal needed to be 
added to the pots as the small pots in this experiment needed 4.3g of bone meal to produce the 
suggested application rate. Most likely bringing bone meal on the spacecraft to the Moon would not be 
cost effective for producing cost efficient and sustainable growth. Based on this research, adding 
mycorrhizal fungi – specifically Glomus intraradices (Rhizophagus irregularis) and Glomus mosseae - 
would not be a beneficial choice for plant growth; however, further research is needed to corroborate 
this statement. The biggest takeaways from this experiment is the information gained from researching 
additional experimental factors and measurements that could be done in future experiments including 
the adjustment of the soil pH, adding in potassium, determining if the fungi form a symbiotic 
relationship with the roots of the mung beans, measuring the color of the leaves, and measuring the 
photosynthetic rate.
